power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Given 14 trials and substantial heterogeneity, the test had low power, so the small-study effects can be neither confirmed nor ruled out (see also the funnel plot: Figure 3). Note. Each point is one effect size (k = 230 from 14 trials). The dashed vertical line is the pooled estimate from the three-level model (g = 0.42). Shaded bands show pseudo-confidence regions (unshaded outside the darkest band: p < .01). Effect sizes from the same trial have similar standard errors, which produces horizontal banding, and the plot should be read with this dependence in mind.

Overall, the confidence intervals ranged from narrow (e.g., multimodal training [0.18, 0.25], six trials with consistent effects) to wide (e.g., immediate post-intervention [0.07, 0.75], where trials differed substantially). Narrow intervals from separately fitted subgroups may understate uncertainty. In addition, all these results should be viewed as inconclusive due to low power rather than confirmed effect or absences of effect, given that 80% power at n=14 would require R² ≈ 36%. Moreover, concerns on collinearity between moderators are not neglected, especially between overall academic achievement/functioning and informer types (bias-corrected Cramér's V = .54; simulated p = .013) and intervention types and people involved in the intervention (bias-corrected Cramér's V = .45; simulated p = .057). The independent effect of moderators cannot be assumed.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

text.text: Children and young people (CYP) with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) often face inequalities when accessing learning opportunities.
The evidence base is mixed on the effectiveness of school-based interventions for CYP with ADHD on academic progress gains and improved attendance.
We conducted a meta-analysis to specify whether school-based interventions improve the educational outcomes of CYP with ADHD.
Seven databases were searched until 2nd of October 2026.
The review followed the PRISMA guidelines.

Of the 2164 items identified, only 16 studies (14 independent trials) were included in our analysis as they met our inclusion criteria: a) CYP with ADHD aged 5-17 years old; b) school-based interventions; c) randomized controlled trials; and d) educational outcomes.
Given the substantial heterogeneity across intervention types, the findings show an inconclusive pattern of what works and what doesn't.
Our main model demonstrated that overall school-based interventions showed a small effect on educational outcomes amongst CYP with ADHD.
No significant moderators, such as intervention types and outcome domains, were detected.

Future research should examine the broader contextual, educational, and environmental factors associated with better educational outcomes amongst CYP with ADHD, with the aim of developing more evidence-informed and targeted interventions.
Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is one of the most prevalent neurodivergences globally, with around 8% of children and young people (CYP) diagnosed with ADHD (Ayano et al., 2023).

text.text: Academic achievement/performance and functioning are two different concepts which reflect the outcomes of learning (e.g., grades and test scores), and processes and behaviours that enable that learning (e.g., homework management skills and concentration).

A number of studies argue that CYP with ADHD demonstrate sub-optimal performance in reading, writing, math and overall grade point average (GPA) and have higher rates of grade retention and dropout when compared to autistic peers or those without ADHD (Arnold et al., 2020; Henning et al., 2022; Jangmo et al., 2019; Kent et al., 2011; Mayes et al., 2020; Niemi et al., 2022; Schmengler et al., 2023; Sibley et al., 2014).

text.text: Despite the limited evidence base on predictors of educational outcomes amongst CYP with ADHD, interventions are developed to support these young people with learning.

Such interventions involve varied programmes and happen across different settings, which can be classified into pharmacological treatments (Jangmo et al., 2019), educational instructions/accommodations (Lovett & Nelson, 2021), psychosocial interventions (e.g., behavioural managements, cognitive/organizational skill training and neurofeedback) (Tresco et al., 2010), physiological treatments (e.g., exercise) (Den Heijer et al., 2017) and multimodal interventions, which combine two or more different types of therapies or strategies, such as medication (Hinshaw et al., 2015).

text.text: Although ADHD medication (e.g., methylphenidate) has been found to be effective at improving inattention and executive function and considered as the first line of treatment (Wolraich et al., 2019), a handful of studies showed a small to medium effect on improving reading and math performance (Gosling et al., 2025).

text.text: Behavioural management (i.e. contingency management) is the most common psychosocial intervention for CYP with ADHD (Danielson et al., 2018; Chacko et al., 2024; Shrestha et al., 2020), although its fidelity, scalability and sustainability has been questioned (Kates & LaFreniere, 2025).

text.text: Digital cognitive training is another popular intervention modality.

However, recent reviews showed that the studies of digital interventions suffered from commercial and regulatory concerns, although potential benefits on inattention and executive function might exist (Evans et al., 2021; Gabarron et al., 2025; Simons et al., 2016).

text.text: Generally, computerized cognitive trainings were largely criticized by weak evidence, limited real-world transfer results, short-term effectiveness and over-reliance on screen time, which leads to physical discomfort and emotion reactions (Westwood et al., 2023).

text.text: Lastly, few studies on multimodal interventions with the combinations of multiple behaviour management strategies and medication showed superior results to either one (Catalá-López et al., 2017; Öğütlü et al., 2024; The MTA Cooperative Group, 1999), presenting inconsistent findings that require further research (Peterson et al., 2024).

text.text: To date, the evidence base has primarily focused on proximal ADHD symptoms instead of distal functioning outcomes (e.g., Türk et al., 2023).
text.formatted: To date, the evidence base has primarily focused on proximal ADHD symptoms instead of distal functioning outcomes (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">Türk et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The ultimate goals of treatment should be functional remissions (Sasser et al., 2017); however, drawing associations between symptoms and functioning does not solve the problem, but rather reinforces false narratives (Weiss et al., 2018; Weiss, 2022).
text.formatted: The ultimate goals of treatment should be functional remissions <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">(Sasser et al., 2017)</ref>; however, drawing associations between symptoms and functioning does not solve the problem, but rather reinforces false narratives <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">(Weiss et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">Weiss, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, addressing the needs of CYP with ADHD should go beyond the core symptoms of ADHD and focus on the needs and capabilities of CYP with ADHD.

The current meta-analysis aims to integrate evidence from randomized-controlled trials (RCT) that evaluated the impact of school-based interventions on educational outcomes exclusively in CYP with ADHD and obtain a robust estimate of the effect of different psychosocial and multimodal treatments.

Meta-analyses that include RCTs alone have higher reliability and lower risk of selection bias (Fabiano et al., 2015), when compared to the ones that had within group or single subject designs (DuPaul et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Meta-analyses that include RCTs alone have higher reliability and lower risk of selection bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Fabiano et al., 2015)</ref>, when compared to the ones that had within group or single subject designs <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(DuPaul et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Randomised, controlled comparisons also support causal inference about average effects, which are not comparable with single-case effect sizes using within-person variances (Saldanha et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Randomised, controlled comparisons also support causal inference about average effects, which are not comparable with single-case effect sizes using within-person variances <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">(Saldanha et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In addition, previous reviews were often looking at academic skills (Yegencik et al., 2025, although the primary outcomes were ADHD symptoms) or one specific type of intervention (e.g., organizational skills training) (Bikic et al., 2017), overlooked overall academic achievement and other modalities and the comparable effect among them.
text.formatted: In addition, previous reviews were often looking at academic skills <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">(Yegencik et al., 2025</ref>, although the primary outcomes were ADHD symptoms) or one specific type of intervention (e.g., organizational skills training) <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bikic et al., 2017)</ref>, overlooked overall academic achievement and other modalities and the comparable effect among them.

text.text: Thus, this meta-analysis comprehensively includes school-based interventions and investigates potential predictors and moderators of treatment effects including intervention types and follow-up periods etc.

By isolating educational outcomes as the primary focus, it clarifies the extent to which non-pharmacological treatments can improve learning outcomes and skills, addressing a major gap in ADHD intervention research.
The present meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses (PRISMA) guidance.
The protocol was registered in the Open Science Framework (Zhang et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The protocol was registered in the Open Science Framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">(Zhang et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Eligibility criteria for studies included: ADHD CYP or CYP with ADHD traits, aged from 5 to 17 years old (primary or secondary school students), primarily examined the effectiveness of non-pharmacological interventions to improve educational outcomes, provided effect sizes or sufficient information to calculate effect sizes by hand and were RCTs, primarily based in school (may have a home/parent component), peer reviewed, written in English, and quantitative.

Pharmacological or neurofeedback interventions (e.g. electroencephalography) were excluded, given that the main aim of this meta-analysis is to evaluate the effectiveness of interventions beyond person's deficits.
Qualitative research, conference papers, commentaries, letters, editorials, theses, and extended abstracts were excluded.
No restrictions were applied on the publication dates of the studies.

Studies were searched by titles, abstracts, and/or keywords strategies through seven databases: EBSCOhost, PubMed, PsycINFO, Scopus, Web of science, ASSIA, and Google scholar on the 9 th of June 2025.

The search was repeated on the 2nd of October 2026, with the following search strings: ("attention deficit hyperactivity disorder" OR ADHD) AND (child* OR adolescent* OR youth OR "school-aged") AND ("academic achievement" OR "academic performance" OR "school performance" OR grades OR GPA OR "test scores" OR "standardized tests") AND ("educational intervention" OR "academic intervention" OR "instructional strategy" OR "teaching strategy" OR "school-based intervention" OR "learning support" OR "instructional support") AND ("effectiveness" OR "treatment effect" OR "outcome evaluation" OR "intervention study" OR "evidence-based" OR "RCT" OR "randomized controlled trial").
The term "test scores" and "standardized tests" contain tests on both academic achievement and functioning, such as Woodcock-Johnson III and The Homework Problems Checklist.
Studies also tended to mix academic achievement and functioning in their measurements and analyses (e.g. DuPaul et al., 2006).
text.formatted: Studies also tended to mix academic achievement and functioning in their measurements and analyses (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">DuPaul et al., 2006)</ref>.

text.text: DZ independently screened the papers against the above inclusion and exclusion criteria.
A randomly assigned 10% of titles/abstracts and 15% full texts were screened by DH to calculate inter-rater reliability with DZ.
The Cohen's K was 0.77 (substantial) for titles/abstracts, and 0.72 (substantial) for full texts (McHugh, 2012).
text.formatted: The Cohen's K was 0.77 (substantial) for titles/abstracts, and 0.72 (substantial) for full texts <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(McHugh, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Any discrepancies were resolved through discussion between the two researchers and OP and VS made final decisions if needed.
The revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomized trials (RoB 2) was used to assess the quality of each trial and the risk of bias (Sterne et al., 2019).
text.formatted: The revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomized trials (RoB 2) was used to assess the quality of each trial and the risk of bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">(Sterne et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: DZ independently assessed the quality of each paper and rated their scores on each dimension (randomization process, deviations from the intended interventions, missing outcome data, measurement of the outcome, selection of the reported result).
DZ then extracted the data including sample sizes, ages, intervention type, academic domains, effect sizes, and standard errors, etc. for data synthesis and further analysis.
All analyses were conducted in R (Version: 4.5.1), using package "metafor", "meta" and "clubSandwich".
To calculate the effect sizes, sample sizes, means and standard deviations in intervention and control groups were extracted across different measurement points and follow up periods.
Hedges' g instead of Cohen's d was computed to quantify the differences between groups to adapt small sample sizes of studies.

The educational outcome domains were coded into 2 overall academic achievement/performance and academic functioning categories and 9 sub-categories in the same direction with higher scores indicating better educational outcomes across: reading, mathematics, writing, academic productivity, academic organization/executive function, academic engagement/classroom functioning, school attendance/conduct problems, global academic performance/achievement, and global academic functioning.

The intervention types were based on the primary component and were coded as physical exercise, study and organizational skill training, cognitive training, behaviour training and multimodal, which mixes at least two aspects of other four types of interventions (not medications).

A random effect three-level meta-analysis was utilized due to heterogeneity and multiple effect sizes extracted from the same study, using Cluster-Robust Variance Estimation (RVE) to account for small samples.
The I² was computed using Cheung's approach to denote between and within study variances (Cheung, 2014).
text.formatted: The I² was computed using Cheung's approach to denote between and within study variances <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Cheung, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Moderator analyses were performed by the intervention types, measurement timepoints, educational outcome domains, informers (student or student-proxy ratings), school level, people involved in the intervention and risk of bias with cluster-robust variance estimator, type 2 (CR2) robust F-test and Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) FDR adjustments for multiple testing.
The collinearity between moderators was assessed by bias-corrected Cramér's V (Bergsma, 2013), which does not depend on the arbitrary order of the category codes.
text.formatted: The collinearity between moderators was assessed by bias-corrected Cramér's V <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bergsma, 2013)</ref>, which does not depend on the arbitrary order of the category codes.

text.text: Moderator pairs with large associations (V > .40) were considered not separable.
text.formatted: Moderator pairs with large associations (V > .40) were considered not separable.

text.text: Sensitivity analyses were also conducted to detect the robustness of the findings using Leave-One-Study-Out (LOO) strategies for outliers and Dominant Study Removal for sample and weight skew.

Lastly, small-study effects were assessed by funnel plot and adjusted by PET-PEESE tests due to the inapplicability of Trimand-fill and selection models for small numbers of trials and dependent effects per trial.
Normality of the random effects was checked by applying Shapiro-Wilk tests to the empirical Bayes estimates (BLUPs) at each level.

text.text: In total, 14 independent trials from 16 studies were eligible for inclusion in this metaanalysis (Figure 1), with 5 trials with high risk of overall bias, 2 trials with some concerns and 7 trials with low risk of overall bias (see Table S1 for individual ratings of risk of bias).

text.text: The number of trials included was smaller than the previous meta-analyses on school-based interventions (Moore et al., 2018; Richardson et al., 2015), as they also considered students at preschool and further education, theses/dissertations, and biofeedback trainings.

text.text: In this meta-analysis, two hundred and thirty effect sizes were extracted from 14 trials, of which 12 trials were conducted in North America, 1 in Africa, and 1 in Asia.
Sixteen hundred CYP with ADHD were recruited, with the sample size ranging from 29 to 326 in each trial.
All the participants were diagnosed with ADHD except for 2 trials that had CYP with high ratings of ADHD symptoms (Pfiffner et al., 2016; Pfiffner et al., 2018; Ramer et al., 2020).
text.formatted: All the participants were diagnosed with ADHD except for 2 trials that had CYP with high ratings of ADHD symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">(Pfiffner et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Pfiffner et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Ramer et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Nearly 77% of the sample were boys aged around 11.21 years (unweighted).

Around 32.07% of the participants also reported ADHD medications (unweighted) and had co-occurring conditions such as Oppositional Defiant Disorder (ODD), Conduct Disorder (CD), anxiety, depression and learning differences.
Seven trials were conducted in primary schools, and the other seven trials were in secondary schools.

In terms of people involved in the intervention (excluding researchers, mentors or coaches), five trials had CYP with ADHD only, with another 3 trials had both CYP with ADHD and parents, 2 trials had CYP with ADHD and teachers, and 4 trials had CYP with ADHD, parents and teachers.

As for intervention types, two interventions were categorized as physical exercises, two as study and organizational skill trainings, two as cognitive trainings, two as behaviour trainings and six as multimodal.
Lastly, 57% of effect sizes used CYP with ADHD-proxy ratings on educational outcomes, with only 43% based on CYP with ADHD's own performance.
The educational outcome measurement times were from during treatment, immediately post treatment to a year and the intervention duration and frequency varied from trial to trial (Table 1 & 2   2).

To further explore potential sources of between-trial variability, subgroup analyses examined intervention type, educational outcome domain, informer type, measurement timepoint, school level, people involved in the intervention and risk of bias as moderators (Table 3).

text.text: However, none of the moderators were significant.

Looking at the subgroup pooled estimates, significant effects were observed for study and organisational skills training (g = .57, 95% CI [0.33, 0.82], p < .001) and multimodal training (g = .22, 95% CI [0.18, 0.25], p < .001).

text.text: Significant effects were also observed for academic organisation/executive functioning (g = .37, 95% CI [0.24, 0.49], p < .001), academic productivity/homework performance (g = .19, 95% CI [0.10, 0.28], p < .001), global academic functioning (g = .18, 95% CI [0.12, 0.24], p < .001) and overall academic functioning (g = .21, 95% CI [0.08, 0.35], p < .001).

text.text: In contrast, effects were not statistically significant for the remaining intervention types or outcome domains.
For the informer types, the significant effect was only observed in student-proxy ratings (g = .21, 95% CI [0.06, 0.36], p = .006).

For measurement timepoint, significant effects were observed during the intervention (g = .26, 95% CI [0.07, 0.46], p = .008), immediately post-intervention (g = .41, 95% CI [0.07, 0.75], p = .017), and at follow-up (g = .24, 95% CI [0.18, 0.31], p < .001).

text.text: Lastly, significant effects were found in secondary school (g = .28, 95% CI [0.11, 0.45], p = .002), involving students and parents (g = .26, 95% CI [0.14, 0.37], p < .001), or students, teachers and parents in the interventions (g = .20, 95% CI [0.14, 0.26], p < .001) (Table 4).

text.text: Overall, the confidence intervals ranged from narrow (e.g., multimodal training [0.18, 0.25], six trials with consistent effects) to wide (e.g., immediate post-intervention [0.07, 0.75], where trials differed substantially).
Narrow intervals from separately fitted subgroups may understate uncertainty.
In addition, all these results should be viewed as inconclusive due to low power rather than confirmed effect or absences of effect, given that 80% power at n=14 would require R² ≈ 36%.

Moreover, concerns on collinearity between moderators are not neglected, especially between overall academic achievement/functioning and informer types (bias-corrected Cramér's V = .54; simulated p = .013) and intervention types and people involved in the intervention (bias-corrected Cramér's V = .45; simulated p = .057).
The independent effect of moderators cannot be assumed.
Sensitivity analyses were conducted to assess the robustness of the primary estimate.

Restricting the analysis to trials assessed as having a low risk of bias (n = 7) produced a comparable effect estimate (g = .35), although the confidence interval crossed zero (95% CI [-0.25, 0.95], robust p = .22).
The corresponding prediction interval was also wide and crossed zero (95% PI [-0.98, 1.68]), indicating substantial residual uncertainty in the expected effect across new trials.
A leave-one-trial-cluster-out analysis was subsequently conducted across 14 iterations.
The pooled effect estimates ranged from g = .30 to g = .47.

Hattabi (2022) and Dai (2025) were the most influential trials, with their removal resulting in the largest reduction in the pooled estimate (g = .31, 95% CI [0.001, 0.62] and g = .30, 95% CI [0.01, 0.58]).
Thus, the overall conclusion of a small positive effect was robust in direction but sensitive in magnitude (Table 5).

text.text: A further sensitivity analysis examined the influence of the three largest trials.

Removing Evans (2016) resulted in g = .43 (95% CI [0.04, 0.83], p = .04), DuPaul (2006)/Jitendra (2007) resulted in g = .44 (95% CI [0.05, 0.84], p = .03), and while removal of DuPaul (2021) resulted in g = .43 (95% CI [0.04, 0.83], p = .04).

text.text: Removing all three trials produced g = .49 (95% CI [0.01, 0.97], p = .047).
These estimates were comparable to the primary analysis, suggesting that the pooled effect was not substantially influenced by any of the largest trials.

However, the three largest trials produced a smaller and consistent average unweighted effect (mean g ≈ 0.18, with little variation between trials: I² = 44%), whereas the remaining 11 smaller trials averaged unweighted g ≈ 0.41 with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 92%).

The BLUPs results demonstrated that the effect-size-level random effects showed no departure from normality (W = .993, p = .361), but trial-level random effects did (W = .762, p = .002), likely reflecting a small number of high-effect trials.
This meta-analysis aimed to evaluate whether, and which, school-based interventions are most effective for improving academic achievement and functioning in CYP with ADHD.
Overall, the results showed that the school-based interventions had a small effect on CYP with ADHD's educational outcomes.

However, there was substantial heterogeneity within and between studies limiting our ability to examine moderators such as intervention types, outcome domains, informant, measurement timepoints, school level, people involved and risk of bias.
Subgroup estimates were generally small and positive, and differences between subgroups could not be established.

These findings were comparable with previous reviews (Moore et al., 2018; Richardson et al., 2015), which demonstrated small improvements on CYP with ADHD's scholastic behaviours and outcomes using school-based interventions and little evidence for moderation, with daily report cards outperforming study and organisation skills training for teacher-rated academic outcomes (Moore et al., 2018) and social skills training and longer intervention durations associating with smaller effects on teacher-rated school adjustment (Richardson et al., 2015).
text.formatted: These findings were comparable with previous reviews <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Moore et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Richardson et al., 2015)</ref>, which demonstrated small improvements on CYP with ADHD's scholastic behaviours and outcomes using school-based interventions and little evidence for moderation, with daily report cards outperforming study and organisation skills training for teacher-rated academic outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Moore et al., 2018)</ref> and social skills training and longer intervention durations associating with smaller effects on teacher-rated school adjustment <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">(Richardson et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Our sub-analyses highlighted that significant effects of school-based interventions were observed in improving academic functioning, with the evidence for academic achievement being inconclusive.

The review by Yegencik et al. (2025) partially echoed these findings, where academic skills of CYP with ADHD measured by standardised tests, grades, and non-standardised measures were improved using school-based approaches.
text.formatted: The review by <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">Yegencik et al. (2025)</ref> partially echoed these findings, where academic skills of CYP with ADHD measured by standardised tests, grades, and non-standardised measures were improved using school-based approaches.

text.text: From the studies reviewed here, many interventions solely concerned CYP with ADHD and applied a within-person deficit model to modify their behavior and increase their attention.

As academic achievement serves as a direct outcome of academic functioning (DuPaul et al., 2011; Jangmo et al., 2019), the promoted academic skills of CYP with ADHD should result in better academic achievement.
text.formatted: As academic achievement serves as a direct outcome of academic functioning <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(DuPaul et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Jangmo et al., 2019)</ref>, the promoted academic skills of CYP with ADHD should result in better academic achievement.

text.text: However, this meta-analysis could not confirm this link, as the evidence for academic achievement was imprecise rather than absent.

This raises questions about the current focus on the individuals and prompts broader considerations on classroom accommodations, modifications and contextual support, given the multiple predictors of academic achievement beyond CYP with ADHD (Zhang et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This raises questions about the current focus on the individuals and prompts broader considerations on classroom accommodations, modifications and contextual support, given the multiple predictors of academic achievement beyond CYP with ADHD <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">(Zhang et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, increasing CYP with ADHD's academic functioning might not be enough to help them achieve better in academics, unless accompanied by a suitable environment and support means which allow them to thrive.

Balancing the intervention focus between CYP with ADHD and the wider contexts such as school environment and family resources could holistically promote overall educational outcomes instead of academic functioning alone (Hulsbosch et al., 2025; Langberg et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Balancing the intervention focus between CYP with ADHD and the wider contexts such as school environment and family resources could holistically promote overall educational outcomes instead of academic functioning alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Hulsbosch et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Langberg et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Multimodal training programmes showed small but consistent effects, although they did not outperform other intervention types.
The systematic support, for example, which combines organisational trainings and contingency management, may be necessary to assist CYP with ADHD to learn (Langberg et al., 2008).
text.formatted: The systematic support, for example, which combines organisational trainings and contingency management, may be necessary to assist CYP with ADHD to learn <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Langberg et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Although, this meta-analysis did not consider medications, previous research also noted that integrated interventions with ADHD medical treatment may be superior to other modality or medication alone, achieving higher compliance and family satisfaction (Enns et al., 2017; Lv et al., 2023).

text.text: While the prevalence of CYP with ADHD receiving multimodal treatments was comparably low (Riedel et al., 2021), direct comparisons of multimodal and single-component programmes in schools are needed.

text.text: The meta-analysis had high heterogeneities in the type and delivery of interventions, which is a common issue in ADHD intervention research (DuPaul et al., 2012).

text.text: Studies also varied greatly from fidelity, intervention duration, control condition and ADHD sample characteristics, including CYP's medication status, which hindered further comparisons of different intervention modalities to understand what interventions work for whom to design interventions (Abikoff, 2009).

text.text: It is also worth noting that none of the moderators are significant to explain the effectiveness of the interventions, probably due to limited statistical power available with 14 trials.
Larger primary research, and future meta-analyses with greater number of studies, are needed before moderators of intervention effectiveness can be ruled in or out.

In parallel, research directly examining how school-level factors relate to educational outcomes in CYP with ADHD would help clarify whether contextual effects are large enough to warrant tailoring intervention choice by setting (Zhang et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In parallel, research directly examining how school-level factors relate to educational outcomes in CYP with ADHD would help clarify whether contextual effects are large enough to warrant tailoring intervention choice by setting <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">(Zhang et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Policymakers and practitioners should be cautious about recommending any specific school-based interventions for CYP with ADHD in a particular context.

Based on the Practice Model of National Association of School Psychologists (NASP, 2020), school psychologists can reasonably consider these interventions as one component of academic support for CYP with ADHD without choosing one approach over another as no intervention type or school level etc. showed an advantage under small-sample inferences.
Rather, selection should follow the student's needs, context, and feasibility and with the consultations and collaborations of teachers and families.

For policy, administrators and policymakers can treat the results as modest support for continued investment in school-based programs targeting academic functioning of CYP with ADHD (e.g. organisation and homework skills).
Fundings should also be placed on intervention studies exploring contextual support for CYP with ADHD.

For further research, researchers can strengthen the evidence base by reporting school characteristics, CYP with ADHD's characteristics (including co-occurring conditions, and cultural backgrounds) and multi-informant educational outcomes.
This would allow future moderator analyses, including analyses of whether interventions work equitably across ADHD individuals.

In addition, greater emphasis should be given on CYP with ADHD's own perspectives, exploring how they understand and experience academic progress and whether the outcomes assessed align with their priorities, experiences, and needs.

This is particularly important to ensure that interventions are evaluated not only in terms of externally observed improvements, but also in terms of outcomes that CYP with ADHD themselves recognise as meaningful.

First, we did not test intervention durations, school conditions (mainstream/special), or co-occurring conditions as moderators, due to limited information provided across trials as well as of the small number of trials included in the analysis (n=14).
Research has shown that medication history and co-occurring conditions might be important moderators to behavioural treatment response (MTA Cooperative Group, 1999; Owens et al., 2003).
text.formatted: Research has shown that medication history and co-occurring conditions might be important moderators to behavioural treatment response <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">(MTA Cooperative Group, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Owens et al., 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Second, studies in other languages were not included, limiting the evidence from the global south.

Although ADHD symptomatology, school behaviours, and academic expectations are influenced and differ by culture, translational interventions across countries can also be adapted and used to inform the wider literature (Diener et al., 2025; Ghosh et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Although ADHD symptomatology, school behaviours, and academic expectations are influenced and differ by culture, translational interventions across countries can also be adapted and used to inform the wider literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Diener et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Ghosh et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Lastly, the small-study effects may exist favouring small trials with large effects, or genuine differences between larger and smaller trials in intervention types and outcome measures.

Although the PET-PEESE tests yielded non-significant results, descriptively, the skewed trial-level random effects and the small averaged effects that three largest trials produced may reflect publication or selective-reporting bias.
Finally, with 14 trials, the robust moderator test had very few degrees of freedom and should be interpreted cautiously.

This meta-analysis is distinctive in examining both academic achievement and academic functioning outcomes of school-based interventions for CYP with ADHD, using a three-level model with small-sample robust inference to handle dependent effect sizes.

The available evidence suggests a small effect of school-based interventions on educational outcomes for CYP with ADHD, but with substantial heterogeneity, sensitivity to influential studies and unresolved publication-bias uncertainty.
No moderator reliably explained differences between trials, and the number of trials is too small to say whether any of them matter.
The evidence is inconclusive, with some effects observed in organisational and multimodal trainings and in academic functioning.
Conclusions on how we should tailor school-based interventions for CYP with ADHD need larger and more consistently reported trials.
